newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Labour wants action on high NZ dlr as talks drag.
newsitem.headline: Labour wants action on high NZ dlr as talks drag.

text.p: New Zealand's opposition Labour party said on Monday the country was losing patience with the political stalemate, and urgent action was needed to tackle an overvalued currency.
Labour met the nationalist New Zealand First party for a fresh round of coalition talks aimed at forming a coalition government, more than seven weeks after an inconclusive general election.
New Zealand First is also negotiating with the conservative National Party caretaker government, and still refuses to say which way it will jump.
"The clock's ticking on," Labour leader Helen Clark told reporters. "I think the country has got a sense of impatience."

Labour, which ran a strong campaign promising more funding for health and education, appeared front-runner after the October 12 general election to lead a government with support from New Zealand First.

NZ First leader Winston Peters has generally been seen as closer to Labour on social and Maori policy. But he fuelled speculation he may yet lean towards National with a speech on Sunday saying whatever the party decided, many supporters would be disappointed.
As Treasury released a fresh set of economic forecasts, Labour finance spokesman Michael Cullen renewed calls for urgent steps to rein in the high-flying New Zealand dollar.
In a speech to businessmen, Cullen said the currency had become a one-way bet through being "systematically overvalued", and more than just a fall in interest rates was required to correct it.

"If we do not achieve a significant correction in the exchange rate before Christmas, then it is all too possible that the economic outlook could turn bleak indeed at some stage in 1997," Cullen warned.
The currency has hit a series of eight-and-a-half-year highs in recent weeks as investors flock to take advantage of high real interest rates.
Treasury forecast 2.6 percent GDP growth in the year to March, little changed from September's projection of 2.5 percent.
It projected a budget operating surplus of NZ$2.49 billion (US$1.78 billion) in the year to June 1997, down from $2.87 billion forecast in September.
Financial markets largely shrugged off the forecasts, as analysts expect government spending to rise significantly, whatever coalition emerges.

Bankers Trust economists said the growth estimates from Treasury looked optimistic for the current year. They said the main focus would remain on politics and a major central bank statement on December 17. ($1 = NZ$1.40)
